question: Which body, set up in 1938 under the chairmanship of Jawaharlal Nehru, first drew up a comprehensive scheme of economic planning for a free India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The National Planning Committee.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The National Planning Committee was set up in 1938 by the Indian National Congress, under the presidency of Subhas Chandra Bose, with Jawaharlal Nehru as its chairman. (राष्ट्रीय योजना समिति — 1938)

 

• It was the first systematic attempt to draw up a comprehensive plan of economic development for an independent India, and it worked through some 29 sub-committees covering industry, agriculture, power, transport, education and health.

 

• Its recommendations rested on rapid industrialisation and a leading role for the state, and they shaped the thinking behind the Five Year Plans after 1951.

 

• Its work was interrupted by the Second World War and by Nehru's imprisonment; its report was published only in 1949.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The plan documents drawn up before independence — a favourite comparison in examinations:

 

• National Planning Committee (1938) – Congress; chairman Nehru

 

• Bombay Plan (1944) – eight industrialists including J.R.D. Tata, G.D. Birla and Purushottamdas Thakurdas; proposed a large role for the state in heavy industry

 

• People's Plan (1945) – M.N. Roy, for the Indian Federation of Labour; gave priority to agriculture and to the nationalisation of all production

 

• Gandhian Plan (1944) – S.N. Agarwal; village-centred, stressing cottage and small-scale industry

 

• Sarvodaya Plan (1950) – Jayaprakash Narayan, based on Gandhian and Vinoba Bhave's ideas

 

NOTE

 

• The Bombay Plan (Option 1): Drawn up in 1944 by industrialists, not by the Congress, and six years later than the committee in question.

 

• The Gandhian Plan (Option 2): S.N. Agarwal's plan of 1944, built on the village economy — the opposite of the industrial emphasis of the National Planning Committee.

 

• The People's Plan (Option 3): M.N. Roy's plan of 1945, which differed sharply from Nehru's by putting agriculture first.

question: In which year did Nadir Shah invade India and sack Delhi?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1739.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nadir Shah, the ruler of Persia, invaded India and sacked Delhi in 1739, during the reign of the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah "Rangeela". (नादिर शाह का आक्रमण — 1739)

 

• He defeated the Mughal army at the Battle of Karnal in February 1739, and entered Delhi soon afterwards.

 

• A rumour of his death led to a rising in the city, and Nadir Shah ordered a general massacre — the qatl-e-aam — in which many thousands were killed in a single day.

 

• He carried away the Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus) of Shah Jahan and the Koh-i-Noor diamond, along with treasure of enormous value.

 

• The invasion did not annex territory, but it shattered the prestige of the Mughal empire and exposed its military weakness to every rival power in India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nadir Shah's invasion was followed by the repeated raids of Ahmad Shah Abdali between 1748 and 1767, which completed the ruin of Mughal authority in the north.

 

NOTE

 

• 1707 (Option 2): The year of Aurangzeb's death, conventionally taken as the beginning of the Mughal decline.

 

• 1757 (Option 3): The year of the Battle of Plassey, in which Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah and laid the foundation of British power in Bengal.

 

• 1761 (Option 4): The year of the Third Battle of Panipat, in which Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated the Marathas — a defeat that removed the last Indian power capable of resisting the British.

question: Which philosopher propounded the doctrine of "Dvaita" or dualism?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Madhvacharya.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Madhvacharya (1238-1317) propounded the philosophy of DVAITA, or dualism. (द्वैत — मध्वाचार्य)

 

• Its central claim is that God (Brahman) and the individual soul (Jiva) are two entirely distinct and eternally separate realities. The soul is dependent on God but never becomes one with Him, even after liberation.

 

• Madhvacharya was born at Pajaka near Udupi in Karnataka, and identified Brahman with Vishnu. His school is also called Brahma Sampradaya or Sadvaishnavism.

 

• His principal works are the Anuvyakhyana and his commentaries on the Brahma Sutras and the Bhagavad Gita.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The schools of Vedanta and their founders — the standard comparison:

 

• Advaita (non-dualism) – Shankaracharya; Brahman alone is real, the world is *maya*, and the soul is Brahman

 

• Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism) – Ramanujacharya; the soul and the world are real, but form the body of Brahman

 

• Dvaita (dualism) – Madhvacharya; God and soul are eternally distinct

 

• Dvaitadvaita (dualistic non-dualism) – Nimbarkacharya

 

• Shuddhadvaita (pure non-dualism) – Vallabhacharya

 

• Achintya Bheda Abheda (inconceivable difference and non-difference) – Chaitanya Mahaprabhu

 

NOTE

 

• Shankaracharya (Option 1): Propounded Advaita, the exact philosophical opposite. He established the four mathas at Sringeri, Puri, Dwarka and Badrinath.

 

• Ramanujacharya (Option 2): Propounded Vishishtadvaita, a middle position between the other two, and was deeply influenced by the Alvar saints of the Tamil country.

 

• Nimbarkacharya (Option 4): Propounded Dvaitadvaita, and was a devotee of Radha-Krishna.

question: Which blood group is described as the "universal donor"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is O negative.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• O NEGATIVE blood is called the "universal donor". (सर्वदाता — O निगेटिव)

 

• The reason lies in what its red cells lack. They carry neither the A nor the B antigen, and no Rh (D) antigen either. Since there is nothing on the cell for the recipient's antibodies to attack, it may be given to a person of any group in an emergency.

 

• Conversely, AB POSITIVE is the "universal recipient" — its plasma contains neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies, so it can receive blood of any group.

 

• The rule to remember: the donor is decided by the antigens on the red cells; the recipient by the antibodies in the plasma.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The ABO blood group system was discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1901, for which he received the Nobel Prize in 1930. He also took part in the discovery of the Rh factor in 1940, named after the rhesus monkey.

 

• Antigens and antibodies by group:

 

• A – antigen A; anti-B antibodies

 

• B – antigen B; anti-A antibodies

 

• AB – both antigens; no antibodies

 

• O – no antigens; both antibodies

 

• World Blood Donor Day is observed on 14 June, Landsteiner's birthday.

 

NOTE

 

• AB positive (Option 1): The universal RECIPIENT, not the universal donor. The two are constantly confused, and this is the principal trap in the question.

 

• B negative (Option 2): Carries the B antigen, which would be attacked by the anti-B antibodies present in the plasma of groups A and O.

 

• A positive (Option 3): Can be given only to recipients of groups A and AB who are Rh positive.

question: "Burzahom", the Neolithic site known for its pit dwellings, is located in which region?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kashmir.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Burzahom lies about 16 km from Srinagar in the KASHMIR valley, and is the most important Neolithic site of northern India. (बुर्जहोम — कश्मीर)

 

• Its distinguishing feature is the pit dwelling — deep pits dug into the ground, narrow at the top and wide at the bottom, with steps cut into the side and a roof of birch bark and thatch. These were dug to survive the severe Kashmiri winter, and are found nowhere else in India.

 

• Two further finds make the site remarkable:

 

• The burial of dogs along with their masters — the only such practice known from Neolithic India

 

• A stone slab engraved with a hunting scene, showing two suns or a sun and a moon, which some have read as the record of an astronomical event

 

• The name Burzahom means "the place of birch" in Kashmiri.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Neolithic sites of India worth knowing:

 

• Burzahom and Gufkral – Kashmir; pit dwellings

 

• Mehrgarh – Balochistan; the earliest evidence of farming in the subcontinent

 

• Chirand – Bihar; bone tools

 

• Koldihwa and Mahagara – Uttar Pradesh; the earliest evidence of rice cultivation

 

• Utnur and Piklihal – Karnataka; ash mounds from cattle pens

 

• Daojali Hading – Assam

 

NOTE

 

• Ladakh (Option 1): Its principal archaeological remains are the rock carvings and petroglyphs of the Indus valley, not Neolithic pit dwellings.

 

• Himachal Pradesh (Option 3): Best known archaeologically for its early temples and rock-cut shrines, notably Masroor.

 

• Uttarakhand (Option 4): Known for the Lakhudiyar rock paintings near Almora, which belong to a different tradition.

question: "Rakhigarhi", the largest Harappan site found in India, is located in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Haryana.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rakhigarhi is in the Hisar district of HARYANA, on the bank of the dried-up Drishadvati river, and is the largest Harappan site in India. (राखीगढ़ी — हरियाणा)

 

• The site covers about 350 hectares across seven mounds, which makes it larger than Mohenjodaro and among the largest Harappan settlements anywhere.

 

• It shows the full sequence of the civilisation — Early, Mature and Late Harappan — which is what gives it its importance for dating.

 

• In 2015 an ancient skeleton excavated here yielded DNA, and the analysis published in 2019 found no trace of Central Asian steppe ancestry, a finding much discussed in the debate on Harappan origins.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Harappan sites in India, by state:

 

• Haryana – Rakhigarhi, Banawali, Bhirrana, Mitathal

 

• Gujarat – Lothal, Dholavira, Surkotada, Rangpur

 

• Rajasthan – Kalibangan

 

• Punjab – Ropar (Rupnagar), the first site excavated after independence

 

• Uttar Pradesh – Alamgirpur, the easternmost site

 

• The largest Harappan site overall is Mohenjodaro, in Sindh in present-day Pakistan.

 

NOTE

 

• Punjab (Option 2): Site of Ropar (Rupnagar) on the Sutlej, the first Harappan site excavated in independent India.

 

• Rajasthan (Option 3): Site of Kalibangan, famous for its ploughed field and its fire altars.

 

• Gujarat (Option 4): Site of the greatest number of Harappan settlements, including Dholavira and Lothal — but the largest single site in India is Rakhigarhi.

question: "Nautanki", the folk theatre form performed through the night with song, verse and drum, is associated chiefly with which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Uttar Pradesh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Nautanki is the great folk theatre of UTTAR PRADESH, and was once the most popular form of entertainment across the whole Hindi-speaking belt. (नौटंकी — उत्तर प्रदेश)

 

• It is an operatic form: the story is carried almost entirely in sung verse, in metres such as the *doha*, *chaubola* and *bahr-e-tabeel*, and the performance runs through the night in the open air.

 

• Its characteristic instrument is the nagara, a large kettledrum, whose beating summons the audience and drives the performance.

 

• Its two principal styles are the Kanpur and the Hathras schools. Gulab Bai was its most celebrated performer, and the first woman to appear on the Nautanki stage.

 

• Its subjects are drawn from romance and legend — *Amar Singh Rathore*, *Laila Majnu*, *Sultana Daku* — and from history.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Folk theatre forms of India and their states:

 

• Nautanki – Uttar Pradesh; Swang and Saang – Haryana

 

• Bhavai – Gujarat; Tamasha – Maharashtra

 

• Jatra – West Bengal; Bidesia – Bihar

 

• Yakshagana – Karnataka; Therukoothu – Tamil Nadu

 

• Maach – Madhya Pradesh; Pandavani – Chhattisgarh

 

NOTE

 

• Bihar (Option 1): Known for Bidesia, the theatre of migration created by Bhikhari Thakur, and for Jat-Jatin.

 

• Punjab (Option 2): Known for Naqal and for the ballad tradition of the Dhadis.

 

• Haryana (Option 4): Known for Saang or Swang, a form closely related to Nautanki and made famous by Pandit Lakhmi Chand. This is the strongest distractor, since the two forms share both metres and subjects.

question: The "Gair" dance, performed by men moving in large circles with sticks during Holi, belongs to which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajasthan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Gair is a folk dance of RAJASTHAN, performed chiefly in the Mewar and Marwar regions during Holi. (गैर नृत्य — राजस्थान)

 

• It is danced by men in large concentric circles, moving in and out and striking wooden sticks together in rhythm, to the beat of the dhol, nagara and bankia.

 

• The dancers wear long pleated tunics called angarkhis that flare out as they turn.

 

• Where the dance is performed by the Bhil community it is known as Gair Ghoomar, in which men and women dance together — an unusual feature in Rajasthani folk dance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Folk dances of Rajasthan:

 

• Ghoomar – by women, of Rajput origin, the best known dance of the state

 

• Kalbeliya – of the snake-charmer community; on the UNESCO intangible heritage list

 

• Kachhi Ghodi – performed on dummy horses, with tales of local bandits

 

• Bhavai – balancing a stack of pots on the head

 

• Chari – dancing with a lighted brass pot on the head

 

• Terah Taali – performed seated, with thirteen manjiras tied to the body

 

NOTE

 

• Gujarat (Option 1): Known for Garba and Dandiya Raas. Dandiya Raas is the closest distractor, since it too uses sticks — but it is danced at Navratri by men and women together, not by men at Holi.

 

• Madhya Pradesh (Option 2): Known for Matki, Grida, Charkula and the Bhagoria festival dances of the Bhils.

 

• Haryana (Option 3): Known for Ghoomar, Khoria, Phag and Dhamal, the last of which is also performed at Holi.

question: The "Medaram Jatara", said to be the largest tribal fair in India, is held in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Telangana.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Medaram Jatara, also called Sammakka Saralamma Jatara, is held at the village of Medaram in the Mulugu district of TELANGANA. (मेदाराम जतरा — तेलंगाना)

 

• It is the largest tribal fair in India, and among the largest religious gatherings in the country after the Kumbh Mela, drawing well over a crore of pilgrims.

 

• It is held once in two years, in the month of Magha (February), and lasts four days.

 

• It honours Sammakka and her daughter Saralamma, tribal goddesses of the Koya community, who are remembered for having led a revolt against the Kakatiya rulers over the levying of tribute during a famine.

 

• A distinctive feature is that pilgrims offer jaggery equal to their own weight, called bangaram or "gold".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Medaram lies within the Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary, and the fair is held in a forest clearing rather than at a temple — there is no permanent shrine, only platforms on which the deities are installed for the four days.

 

NOTE

 

• Chhattisgarh (Option 1): Known for the Bastar Dussehra, which runs for seventy-five days and is the longest festival in India, and for the Madai fairs.

 

• Odisha (Option 3): Known for the Rath Yatra at Puri and for Bali Jatra at Cuttack.

 

• Jharkhand (Option 4): Known for the tribal festivals Sarhul, Karma and Tusu Parab, but not for a fair on this scale.

question: The festival celebrated as "Losar" in Ladakh and across the Himalayan belt marks which occasion?
option_1: The beginning of the new year
option_3: The end of the monsoon rains
solution_text:
The correct answer is The beginning of the new year.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Losar is the NEW YEAR festival of the Tibetan Buddhist world, celebrated in Ladakh, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh (Lahaul-Spiti), and in Tibet, Bhutan and Nepal. (लोसर — नववर्ष)

 

• The word itself says so: "lo" means *year* and "sar" means *new*.

 

• It falls in February or March, at the start of the Tibetan lunar calendar, and is observed for about fifteen days, of which the first three are the most important.

 

• In Ladakh it is celebrated earlier than elsewhere — in December — because a fourteenth-century king, Jamyang Namgyal, advanced it so that his troops could observe the festival before setting out on a winter campaign. The earlier date has been kept ever since.

 

• Its observances include the Chham masked dances in the monasteries, the lighting of butter lamps, and the burning of effigies to drive out the evils of the year that has ended.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• New year festivals across India, all falling in the spring:

 

• Ugadi – Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana

 

• Gudi Padwa – Maharashtra; Puthandu – Tamil Nadu

 

• Vishu – Kerala; Bohag Bihu – Assam

 

• Baisakhi – Punjab; Navreh – Kashmir

 

• Cheti Chand – Sindhi community; Losar – the Himalayan Buddhist belt

 

NOTE

 

• The harvest (Option 2): Marked in the Himalayan region by Losoong in Sikkim, which is a harvest festival and falls in December.

 

• The end of the monsoon (Option 3): No major Himalayan Buddhist festival marks this. The monsoon is in any case slight in Ladakh, which lies in a rain shadow.

 

• The birth of the Buddha (Option 4): Marked by Saga Dawa (in Sikkim) and by Buddha Purnima, which commemorates the birth, enlightenment and death of the Buddha on a single day in the month of Vaisakha.

question: The "Dual Government" in Bengal, under which the Company held the revenue and the Nawab the administration, was brought to an end by _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Warren Hastings.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Dual Government in Bengal was ended in 1772 by Warren Hastings, then Governor of Bengal. (द्वैध शासन का अंत — वारेन हेस्टिंग्स, 1772)

 

• The system had been set up by Robert Clive in 1765, after the Company obtained the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa from the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II by the Treaty of Allahabad.

 

• Under it the Company held the Diwani — the right to collect the revenue — while the Nawab retained the Nizamat, the administration and the criminal justice of the province.

 

• Its vice was that it separated power from responsibility: the Company had the revenue but no duty to govern, and the Nawab had the duty but no money. The result was the disastrous Bengal Famine of 1770, in which about a third of the population of Bengal died.

 

• Hastings abolished the arrangement, took the administration directly into the Company's hands, and moved the treasury from Murshidabad to Calcutta.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General of Bengal under the Regulating Act of 1773. He founded the Calcutta Madrasa (1781) and encouraged the Asiatic Society, and was later impeached in Parliament and acquitted after a trial lasting seven years.

 

NOTE

 

• Robert Clive (Option 1): The man who created the Dual Government in 1765, not the one who ended it. This is the principal trap in the question.

 

• Lord Cornwallis (Option 3): Governor-General 1786-93, known for the Permanent Settlement of 1793, the Cornwallis Code, and the separation of revenue and judicial functions.

 

• Lord Wellesley (Option 4): Governor-General 1798-1805, who introduced the Subsidiary Alliance system and founded Fort William College.

question: The "Thaat" system, which classifies the ragas of Hindustani music into ten parent scales, was devised by _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pandit Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Thaat system was devised by Pandit Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande (1860-1936), the great musicologist of Hindustani music. (थाट पद्धति — विष्णु नारायण भातखंडे)

 

• A thaat is a parent scale of seven notes, from which a family of ragas may be derived. Bhatkhande grouped the whole body of Hindustani ragas under ten thaats:

 

• Bilawal, Kalyan, Khamaj, Bhairav, Purvi, Marwa, Kafi, Asavari, Bhairavi and Todi

 

• His purpose was to bring order to a tradition in which each gharana used its own names and its own descriptions. He travelled across India collecting compositions, and set out his system in the Hindustani Sangeet Paddhati and the Kramik Pustak Malika.

 

• He founded the music college at Lucknow that is now the Bhatkhande Sanskriti Vishwavidyalaya.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Carnatic counterpart of the thaat is the Melakarta, a system of 72 parent scales codified by Venkatamakhin in the 17th century — a far more exhaustive scheme than Bhatkhande's ten.

 

• Bhatkhande and Vishnu Digambar Paluskar are together regarded as the two men who brought Hindustani music out of the courts and into public teaching in the early twentieth century.

 

NOTE

 

• Vishnu Digambar Paluskar (Option 1): The other great reformer of the same generation, who founded the Gandharva Mahavidyalaya at Lahore in 1901 and devised his own system of notation. The similarity of the two men's first names is the trap in this question.

 

• Pandit Ravi Shankar (Option 2): The sitar player who carried Indian music to audiences abroad, and a recipient of the Bharat Ratna. He was a performer, not a musicologist.

 

• Ustad Allauddin Khan (Option 4): The founder of the Maihar Gharana and the teacher of Ravi Shankar, Ali Akbar Khan and Annapurna Devi.

question: Under the Constitution of India, for what maximum period may a Proclamation of Financial Emergency remain in force without the approval of Parliament?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Two months.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A Financial Emergency is proclaimed under Article 360, when the President is satisfied that the financial stability or credit of India or of any part of it is threatened. (वित्तीय आपातकाल — अनुच्छेद 360)

 

• The Proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within TWO MONTHS; if it is not, it ceases to operate.

 

• Once approved, it continues indefinitely — there is no maximum duration, and no further parliamentary approval is required.

 

• Approval requires only a simple majority of each House, not a special majority.

 

• During its operation the Union may direct the States to observe canons of financial propriety, and may reduce the salaries of all public servants, including the judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts.

 

• A Financial Emergency has never been declared in India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three emergencies compared:

 

• National Emergency (Article 352) – approval within one month; then continues for six months at a time. Requires a special majority. Declared three times: 1962, 1971 and 1975.

 

• President's Rule (Article 356) – approval within two months; then six months at a time, up to a maximum of three years. Simple majority.

 

• Financial Emergency (Article 360) – approval within two months; then indefinite. Simple majority. Never declared.

 

• The 44th Amendment (1978) reduced the approval period for a National Emergency from two months to one, and required the Cabinet's written advice before it could be proclaimed.

 

NOTE

 

• One month (Option 1): The period prescribed for a National Emergency under Article 352 — reduced from two months by the 44th Amendment. This is the strongest distractor.

 

• One year (Option 2): Under the 44th Amendment, President's Rule may be extended beyond one year only if a National Emergency is in force or the Election Commission certifies that elections cannot be held.

 

• Six months (Option 3): The period for which a National Emergency or President's Rule continues at a time once approved, not the period for obtaining approval.

question: Who composed the song "Sare Jahan Se Achha", also known as "Tarana-e-Hindi"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Muhammad Iqbal.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Sare Jahan Se Achha", properly titled "Tarana-e-Hindi" (The Anthem of the People of Hindustan), was written by Muhammad Iqbal and first published in 1904 in the weekly *Ittehad*. (सारे जहाँ से अच्छा — मुहम्मद इक़बाल)

 

• It is written in Urdu, in the ghazal form, and celebrates the land of Hindustan as better than all the world.

 

• It was set to its familiar tune by Pandit Ravi Shankar, and is played as a regimental quick march of the Indian Army.

 

• The astronaut Rakesh Sharma quoted its opening line in 1984 when Indira Gandhi asked him how India looked from space.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Patriotic songs and their authors — a set worth memorising:

 

• Vande Mataram – Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay (National Song)

 

• Jana Gana Mana – Rabindranath Tagore (National Anthem)

 

• Sare Jahan Se Achha – Muhammad Iqbal

 

• Jhanda Uncha Rahe Hamara – Shyamlal Gupta 'Parshad'

 

• Sarfaroshi ki Tamanna – Bismil Azimabadi, made famous by Ram Prasad Bismil

 

• Ae Mere Watan Ke Logon – Kavi Pradeep

 

• Saare Jahan Se Achha was written well before Iqbal's later political writing, and its early nationalism is often contrasted with the direction his thought afterwards took.

 

NOTE

 

• Ram Prasad Bismil (Option 1): A revolutionary of the Kakori conspiracy, hanged in 1927. He popularised "Sarfaroshi ki Tamanna", though the verse was written by Bismil Azimabadi.

 

• Shyamlal Gupta 'Parshad' (Option 3): Author of "Jhanda Uncha Rahe Hamara", the flag song adopted by the Congress in 1938.

 

• Rabindranath Tagore (Option 4): Author of "Jana Gana Mana", India's National Anthem, and of Bangladesh's national anthem "Amar Sonar Bangla".

question: The twinkling of stars in the night sky is caused by _____.
option_1: reflection of starlight by dust in the atmosphere
option_3: dispersion of starlight into its colours
solution_text:
The correct answer is atmospheric refraction of starlight.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The twinkling of stars is caused by ATMOSPHERIC REFRACTION — the continuous bending of starlight as it passes through layers of air of different densities. (तारों का टिमटिमाना — वायुमंडलीय अपवर्तन)

 

• A star is so distant that it acts as a point source of light. The air between it and the eye is constantly moving and constantly changing in density and temperature, so the amount by which the light is bent changes from moment to moment.

 

• The result is that the apparent position of the star shifts slightly, and the amount of light entering the eye varies — so the star appears to flicker.

 

• Planets do not twinkle. A planet is much nearer, and is seen as a collection of point sources spread over a small disc. The variations from different points average out, and the light appears steady. This is the standard way of telling a planet from a star with the naked eye.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Atmospheric refraction explains several other everyday effects:

 

• The sun appears about two minutes before actual sunrise and for about two minutes after actual sunset — so the day is lengthened by roughly four minutes.

 

• The sun appears flattened at sunrise and sunset.

 

• The advance appearance of the sun and the shimmering of objects seen over a hot road are both consequences of the same bending.

 

NOTE

 

• Reflection by dust (Option 1): Dust does scatter light and is responsible for haze, but reflection cannot account for the rapid flickering of a point source.

 

• Total internal reflection (Option 2): Occurs when light travelling in a denser medium meets a rarer one beyond the critical angle. It explains the mirage and the working of optical fibres, and does not apply here.

 

• Dispersion (Option 3): The splitting of white light into its colours, as by a prism. Dispersion explains the rainbow, not the twinkling.

question: In India's land-use classification, cultivable land left uncultivated for one to five agricultural years is classified as _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is other fallow.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Land left uncultivated for more than one but less than five agricultural years is classified as OTHER FALLOW (also called *fallow other than current fallow*). (अन्य परती भूमि)

 

• The full set of fallow and waste categories must be distinguished by the length of time the land has lain idle:

 

• Current fallow – left uncultivated for one agricultural year or less

 

• Other fallow – left uncultivated for more than one and up to five years

 

• Culturable waste land – left uncultivated for more than five years, but still capable of being brought under cultivation

 

• Barren and unculturable land – land that cannot be brought under cultivation at all, such as rocky ground, ravines and desert

 

• Land is left fallow so that the soil may recover its natural fertility, a practice as old as agriculture itself.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's land-use categories as reported by the land-use statistics:

 

• Forests

 

• Land put to non-agricultural uses

 

• Barren and unculturable land

 

• Permanent pastures and grazing land

 

• Land under miscellaneous tree crops

 

• Culturable waste land

 

• Fallow other than current fallow

 

• Current fallow

 

• Net sown area

 

• Net sown area plus the area sown more than once gives the gross cropped area. India's cropping intensity is around 140%.

 

NOTE

 

• Current fallow (Option 2): Land left idle for one agricultural year or less — the shortest of the categories, and the strongest distractor here.

 

• Culturable waste land (Option 3): Land left idle for more than five years. It is still capable of cultivation, which is what distinguishes it from the next category.

 

• Barren and unculturable land (Option 4): Land that cannot be cultivated at all, whatever is spent on it — mountain, ravine, rock and desert.

question: Under a system of flexible exchange rates, a fall in the value of the domestic currency against a foreign currency is called _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is depreciation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• DEPRECIATION is a fall in the value of a currency brought about by market forces — the demand for and supply of the currency — under a system of flexible (floating) exchange rates. (मुद्रा का अवमूल्यन एवं मूल्यह्रास)

 

• The essential distinction, and the whole point of the question:

 

• DEPRECIATION – a fall in value under a flexible exchange rate, caused by the market

 

• DEVALUATION – a fall in value under a fixed exchange rate, brought about by a deliberate decision of the government or central bank

 

• The two words describe the same movement; they differ entirely in what causes it.

 

• Correspondingly, a rise in value is called appreciation when it is caused by the market, and revaluation when it is decided by the authorities.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• India has devalued the rupee three times: in 1949, in 1966 (after the failure of the Third Plan and the wars), and in two steps in July 1991 during the balance of payments crisis.

 

• Since 1993 India has followed a managed float, in which the rate is set by the market but the RBI intervenes to smooth excessive volatility.

 

• A depreciating rupee makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers and imports dearer — which is why it raises the cost of India's oil bill.

 

NOTE

 

• devaluation (Option 1): The closest distractor, and the answer most candidates give. It describes the same fall, but as a deliberate act of policy under a fixed rate, not a market movement.

 

• revaluation (Option 3): A deliberate increase in the official value of a currency — the opposite of devaluation.

 

• appreciation (Option 4): A market-driven rise in a currency's value — the opposite of depreciation.

question: Who is the author of the novel "The Guide", which won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1960?
solution_text:
The correct answer is R.K. Narayan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "The Guide" (1958) was written by R.K. Narayan, and won him the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1960 — the first work in English to receive it. (द गाइड — आर.के. नारायण)

 

• It is set, like almost all his fiction, in the imaginary South Indian town of MALGUDI, and follows Raju from tourist guide to convict and at last to reluctant holy man.

 

• It was filmed in 1965 as *Guide*, with Dev Anand and Waheeda Rehman, and the film is among the best known adaptations of an Indian novel.

 

• Narayan's other works include "Swami and Friends", "The Bachelor of Arts", "The English Teacher", "The Man-Eater of Malgudi" and "Malgudi Days". He received the Padma Vibhushan and was nominated to the Rajya Sabha.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Anand, Narayan and Raja Rao are together called the "Big Three" of early Indian writing in English, all of whom began publishing in the 1930s.

 

• Narayan's first novel, *Swami and Friends*, was published in 1935 on the recommendation of Graham Greene, who remained his friend and literary advocate for fifty years.

 

NOTE

 

• Mulk Raj Anand (Option 1): Author of "Untouchable" (1935) and "Coolie" (1936), novels of social protest concerned with caste and poverty.

 

• Raja Rao (Option 2): Author of "Kanthapura" (1938), which tells of the freedom movement reaching a South Indian village, and of the philosophical "The Serpent and the Rope", for which he won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1964.

 

• Kamala Markandaya (Option 4): Author of "Nectar in a Sieve" (1954), a novel of rural poverty and the coming of industry to a South Indian village.

question: Who is the author of the biography "The Life of Mahatma Gandhi"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Louis Fischer.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "The Life of Mahatma Gandhi" (1950) was written by Louis Fischer, an American journalist who had visited Gandhi at Sevagram in 1942 and again in 1946. (द लाइफ ऑफ महात्मा गांधी — लुई फिशर)

 

• It is the standard biography in English and remains the best known, having been written within two years of the assassination and drawing on Fischer's own interviews.

 

• It was the basis of Richard Attenborough's film *Gandhi* (1982), which won eight Academy Awards.

 

• Fischer also wrote "A Week with Gandhi" (1942), an account of his first visit.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Books on Gandhi worth knowing:

 

• "The Story of My Experiments with Truth" – Gandhi's autobiography, written in Gujarati and serialised from 1925

 

• "The Life of Mahatma Gandhi" – Louis Fischer

 

• "Mohandas: A True Story of a Man, His People and an Empire" – Rajmohan Gandhi, his grandson

 

• "Gandhi Before India" and "Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World" – Ramachandra Guha

 

• "Great Soul: Mahatma Gandhi and His Struggle with India" – Joseph Lelyveld

 

• Gandhi's own works also include "Hind Swaraj" (1909) and "Satyagraha in South Africa".

 

NOTE

 

• William Shirer (Option 1): An American journalist who did meet Gandhi and wrote "Gandhi: A Memoir" (1979) — but he is far better known for "The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich". He is the closest distractor here.

 

• Ramachandra Guha (Option 2): Historian, author of the two-volume modern life of Gandhi and of "India After Gandhi".

 

• Rajmohan Gandhi (Option 3): Gandhi's grandson, and the author of "Mohandas" and of biographies of Patel and Rajaji.

question: The Jaisalmer Fort, one of the very few "living forts" in the world, is built chiefly of which stone?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Yellow sandstone.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Jaisalmer Fort is built of YELLOW SANDSTONE, quarried locally, which takes on a deep honey colour in the setting sun. For this reason it is called the "Sonar Quila" or Golden Fort. (सोनार किला — पीला बलुआ पत्थर)

 

• It was built in 1156 by the Bhati Rajput ruler Rawal Jaisal, on Trikuta Hill in the heart of the Thar desert.

 

• It is called a "living fort" because about a quarter of the town's population still lives inside its walls — shops, houses, temples and hotels all within the fortifications. Very few forts anywhere remain inhabited in this way.

 

• It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2013, as part of the group "Hill Forts of Rajasthan".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The "Hill Forts of Rajasthan" inscribed by UNESCO in 2013 are six: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Amber, Jaisalmer and Gagron.

 

• Kumbhalgarh has the second longest continuous wall in the world after the Great Wall of China, running some 36 km.

 

• Satyajit Ray's film "Sonar Kella" (1974) was set at the fort and did much to make it known.

 

NOTE

 

• Red sandstone (Option 1): The material of the Red Fort and the Agra Fort, both built by the Mughals, and of Fatehpur Sikri. It is quarried chiefly around Dholpur and Bharatpur.

 

• White marble (Option 3): The material of the Taj Mahal, quarried at Makrana in Rajasthan, and of the Dilwara Jain temples at Mount Abu.

 

• Granite (Option 4): The material of the great southern temples, such as the Brihadeshwara temple at Thanjavur, and of the rock-cut monuments at Mahabalipuram.

question: The first English factory in India was established at Surat in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1613.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first English factory in India was set up at SURAT in 1613, with the permission of the Mughal emperor Jahangir. (सूरत में पहली अंग्रेजी फैक्ट्री — 1613)

 

• A "factory" in this sense was not a place of manufacture but a fortified warehouse and trading post, where a factor or agent stored goods awaiting shipment.

 

• Permission was obtained after Captain Thomas Best defeated a Portuguese fleet off Swally in 1612, which convinced the Mughal court that the English were worth accommodating.

 

• Sir Thomas Roe arrived as James I's ambassador to Jahangir's court in 1615, and secured wider trading privileges by 1618.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The founding of the three Presidency towns:

 

• Madras (1639) – Francis Day obtained the site from the Raja of Chandragiri and built Fort St. George

 

• Bombay (1661/1668) – came to Charles II as part of the dowry of Catherine of Braganza, and was transferred to the Company in 1668 for a rent of £10 a year

 

• Calcutta (1690) – Job Charnock established the settlement, and Fort William was built in 1700

 

• The European trading companies in India, in order of arrival: Portuguese (1498), Dutch (1602), English (1600), Danish (1616) and French (1664).

 

NOTE

 

• 1600 (Option 2): The year the East India Company was chartered in England by Queen Elizabeth I, on 31 December — thirteen years before the Surat factory. This is the principal trap.

 

• 1639 (Option 3): The year the Company acquired Madras and began building Fort St. George.

 

• 1690 (Option 4): The year Job Charnock founded the settlement that became Calcutta.

question: According to Lindeman's "ten per cent law" of energy transfer in a food chain, what happens at each trophic level?
option_1: Ten per cent of the energy is lost and the remaining ninety per cent is passed on
option_2: Ten per cent of the energy is stored and the rest is converted into new species
option_3: Energy is transferred from one level to the next without any loss whatever
option_4: Only about ten per cent of the energy is passed on to the next trophic level
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only about ten per cent of the energy is passed on to the next trophic level.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The ten per cent law, stated by Raymond Lindeman in 1942, holds that only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next. The remaining 90% is lost. (दस प्रतिशत नियम — लिंडेमैन)

 

• The energy is lost in three ways: as heat in respiration, in the work of metabolism, and in the parts of the organism that are not eaten or not digested.

 

• So if producers hold 10,000 joules, herbivores receive about 1,000, primary carnivores about 100, and top carnivores about 10.

 

• Two important consequences follow, and both are examined:

 

• A food chain rarely has more than four or five trophic levels — beyond that there is too little energy left to support a population.

 

• The number and biomass of organisms decreases at each higher level, which is why the ecological pyramid of energy is always upright.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Energy flow in an ecosystem is unidirectional — it enters as sunlight, passes up the chain and is lost as heat. It cannot be recycled. Nutrients, by contrast, are cycled continuously.

 

• The pyramid of numbers and the pyramid of biomass can be inverted in some ecosystems — a single large tree supporting thousands of insects inverts the pyramid of numbers — but the pyramid of energy is never inverted.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 reverses the proportions, and is the commonest error. It is ninety per cent that is lost, not ten.

 

• Option 2 speaks of energy being "converted into new species", which is not a meaningful process. Energy is stored in biomass, and lost as heat.

 

• Option 3 would mean energy is conserved perfectly through the chain, which contradicts the second law of thermodynamics — some energy is always lost as heat.

question: The Sangam assemblies of Tamil poets are traditionally said to have been held at _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Madurai.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Sangams — assemblies of Tamil poets and scholars — are traditionally said to have been held at MADURAI, under the patronage of the Pandya kings. (संगम — मदुरै)

 

• Tradition speaks of three Sangams:

 

• First Sangam – at Then Madurai (a city said to have been lost to the sea); no work survives

 

• Second Sangam – at Kapatapuram; only the grammar Tolkappiyam survives

 

• Third Sangam – at Madurai; almost the whole of the surviving Sangam literature belongs to it

 

• The literature of the Third Sangam consists chiefly of the Ettuthogai (Eight Anthologies) and the Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls).

 

• The Sangam age is dated roughly to 300 BCE - 300 CE, and its poetry is the principal source for the history of the Chera, Chola and Pandya kingdoms.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sangam poetry is classified by subject into Aham (love, the inner life) and Puram (war, kingship, the outer life).

 

• The Tolkappiyam by Tolkappiyar is the oldest surviving Tamil work, a treatise on grammar and poetics.

 

• The two great Tamil epics, the Silappadikaram (by Ilango Adigal) and the Manimekalai (by Sattanar), belong to the period just after the Sangam age.

 

NOTE

 

• Kanchipuram (Option 1): The Pallava capital, a great centre of temple building and of Sanskrit learning — but not the seat of the Sangams.

 

• Thanjavur (Option 3): The Chola capital from the ninth century, and the site of the Brihadeshwara temple. It rose to importance long after the Sangam age.

 

• Kaveripattinam (Option 4): Also called Puhar, the great port of the early Cholas at the mouth of the Kaveri, and the setting of much of the *Silappadikaram*. It was a centre of trade, not of the poetic assemblies.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

I. Petroleum is separated into its useful constituents by the process of fractional distillation.
II. Coke, obtained from the destructive distillation of coal, is almost pure carbon and is used as a reducing agent in metallurgy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. Petroleum is a mixture of many hydrocarbons, and is separated into its constituents by FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION in a refinery — the mixture is heated and the fractions condense at different heights in the column according to their boiling points. (प्रभाजी आसवन)

 

• The fractions, in ascending order of boiling point: petroleum gas, petrol, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, paraffin wax and bitumen.

 

• Statement II is CORRECT. Coke is obtained by the destructive distillation of coal — heating coal strongly in the absence of air. It is a tough, porous, black substance which is almost pure carbon, and is used as a reducing agent in the extraction of metals, above all iron in the blast furnace.

 

• The destructive distillation of coal yields four products: coke, coal tar, coal gas and ammoniacal liquor.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Petroleum is called "black gold" because of its colour and its value. Its refining in India is carried out by IOCL, BPCL, HPCL and Reliance, among others; the first refinery in India was at Digboi, Assam (1901).

 

• Coal tar is the source of some 200 substances used in making dyes, explosives, paints, plastics, drugs and perfumes. Naphthalene balls, used against moths, are obtained from it.

 

NOTE

 

• Since both statements are correct, Option 1 (Only I), Option 2 (Only II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• Note the distinction between the two processes: fractional distillation separates a mixture without changing its constituents, while destructive distillation decomposes a substance by heating it out of contact with air.

question: Which cell organelle is described as the "kitchen of the cell"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chloroplast.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The CHLOROPLAST is called the "kitchen of the cell", because it is the organelle in which a plant prepares its own food by photosynthesis. (हरितलवक — कोशिका की रसोई)

 

• It contains the green pigment chlorophyll, which traps the energy of sunlight and enables the plant to build glucose from carbon dioxide and water.

 

• It is a double-membraned organelle found only in plant cells and in some protists. Animal cells have none, which is why animals cannot make their own food.

 

• Its internal structure consists of flattened sacs called thylakoids, stacked into grana, suspended in a fluid called the stroma.

 

• Chloroplasts belong to the family of plastids, along with chromoplasts (which give flowers and fruits their colours) and leucoplasts (which store starch, oil and protein).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Like the mitochondrion, the chloroplast is semi-autonomous — it has its own DNA and ribosomes and can make some of its own proteins. This is the basis of the endosymbiotic theory, which holds that both organelles were once free-living bacteria absorbed by an early cell.

 

• Structures found in plant cells but not in animal cells: the cell wall of cellulose, the chloroplast, and a large central vacuole.

 

NOTE

 

• Mitochondrion (Option 1): The "powerhouse" of the cell, where energy is released from food as ATP. Note the distinction that decides this question: the chloroplast makes food, the mitochondrion burns it.

 

• Golgi apparatus (Option 2): The "post office" of the cell, which packages and dispatches the substances made within it.

 

• Ribosome (Option 3): The "protein factory", where amino acids are assembled into proteins. It is the only organelle without a membrane.
